content_voiceover: This case highlights the Jk null phenotype, another example of a difficult-match rare blood type, occurring in roughly one in ten thousand people. Structurally, Jka and Jkb are allelic antigens sitting on the same Kidd glycoprotein, a urea transporter on the red cell membrane. Jk null individuals lack both Jka and Jkb, shown here by a homozygous mutation in intron one on Sanger sequencing, seen classically in Polynesian populations. The clinical problem is that if a Jk null patient is transfused, they can form anti-JK3, an antibody that reacts against essentially every donor red cell that has either Jka or Jkb, making them pan-reactive and nearly untransfusable with ordinary blood. Taiwan actually faced this in 1997, a patient needed Jk-a-b-negative blood, and even after screening over ten thousand potential donors, doctors found only a single compatible donor. That real-world experience is exactly why blood centers now maintain rare donor registries and frozen red cell programs, so a compatible unit can be found quickly in an emergency rather than screening thousands of people from scratch.
keypoints: Jk null phenotype: absent Jka and Jkb antigens, about 1 in 10,000 people
Transfusion risk: anti-JK3 antibody is pan-reactive against nearly all donor RBCs
Taiwan 1997 case: screened over 10,000 donors, found only 1 compatible unit
Rare donor registries and frozen RBC stock now used for emergency matching
